documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) & Machine Learning (ML) are two terms that transformed pharmaceutical sciences, including drug discovery, drug development, precision medicine and nanomedicine. Traditional drug discovery is a long, expensive and failure-prone process that may take over 10 years and million of dollars before it produces a therapeutically active compound ready for clinical trials and commercialization. AI-driven computational approaches can tackle numerous challenges of drug discovery and development, including target or lead identification and optimization, virtual screening, predicting drug target interactions, toxicity and personalized treatment options. The concept of artificial intelligence was first introduced in the 1940s when Alan Turing laid the foundations for machine intelligence theory claiming that there is no fundamental difference between human and machine computation (Turing, 1950). The formal idea of artificial intelligence was further proposed by Mc Carthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon who proposed the Dartmouth Hypothesis about the possibility for machines to stimulate human intelligence (Mc Carthy et al 1955). In the following decades the concepts machine learning and deep learning were introduced Schmidhuber in 2015. There are three review papers that discuss the role of AI&ML in pharmaceutical sciences and health care. The first study focus on the role of artificial intelligence in drug discovery and discovery and precision nanomedicine (Zhu et al, 2022). Zhu et al. highlight importance of algorithms and nano-enabled therapeutics for precision nanomedicine. The main ideas of the study include finding and selecting the target developing the optimal drug using nano-enabled therapeutics and individualizing treatment based on patients characteristics. The second review paper discuss the role of AI in spatial structure of protein predicting and drug synergism prediction targeting molecular mechanism and protein drug interactions (Lie et al, 2022). The study by Lei et al. high-light the importance of AI in analyzing and prediction the spatial structure of protein to reveal molecular mechanisms and biological functions. The third review paper was discusses the concept of artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning elucidates ethical and social implications and high light the public awarness about AI (Garcia & Salichos, 2022). The study by Garcia & Salichosis a detailed analysis about the opportunities and limitations of AI.I would like to address the main ideas of all three reviewed papers and discuss hoe AL&ML can be applied to various stages of drug discovery and development. I will also comment on such terms as machine learning, deep learning, protein spatial structure prediction, virtual screening precision, precision medicine, nanomedicine, drug synergism prediction, explainable AI.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming part of healthcare through tools that help organise medical information, support clinical decisions, answer common questions, and improve communication. These changes affect more than treatment and efficiency: they can also influence how patients feel, how much they trust healthcare professionals, and whether they feel heard and respected. This paper reviews AI in patient–healthcare relationships from a psychosocial perspective. It considers trust, empathy, privacy, patient autonomy, health literacy, anxiety, accessibility, and the role of clinicians in explaining AI-supported decisions. AI can make some services faster and easier to access, but it may also create distance when communication feels automated or when recommendations are difficult to understand. The paper argues that AI should strengthen—not replace—the human relationship at the centre of care. Responsible use requires transparency, protection of personal information, inclusive design, careful evaluation, and meaningful human oversight..

documents.abstract: AI tools are increasingly being utilized in counselling services to provide student support, but their impact on undergraduate students needs to be thoroughly examined. This study examines the relationship between Artificial Intelligence and Counselling Service among Undergraduate Students in Cross River State. To achieve this, three (3) objectives, three (3) research questions and three (3) hypotheses were formulated. Correlational research design was adopted. The sample was 760 students from the sampled faculties out of 44,281 in UNICAL, 31,410 in CRSUE, and 23,971 in UNICROSS. Three experts validated the instrument, it was titled "Usage, Awareness, Attitude towards AI and Effective Counselling Service Questionnaire" and was administered to the respondents to elicit their responses.

This study examines the relationship between the development of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and the rights of older persons. It analyses the opportunities that smart applications offer in health care, independent living, social connection and economic security, set against the risks arising from digital exclusion, algorithmic age discrimination, privacy violations and fraud. The study adopts a descriptive-analytical approach based on international reports, systematic reviews, meta-analyses and relevant national surveys, and discusses the UAE legislative context. The review shows that the age gap in use remains wide, that the evidence of benefits is promising but limited, and that fraud risks are documented by rising figures. The study proposes a preliminary framework for safe digital empowerment that links graduated learning, inclusive design, data protection, human review and evaluation. It concludes that the rights-based value of AI is not measured by the mere availability of a service, but by its capacity to expand the real choices of older persons while respecting their will and dignity. The study does not present field results, nor does it claim to have tested the proposed model. documents.abstract: This research reveals the contemporary British fiction crisis of human identity through a comparative reading of Kazoo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun and Ian McEwan’s Machines Like Me. Both novels view artificial intelligence as more than just a technology, instead, they treat it as a tool for subverting the human-machine divide. According to Adam, humans do not possess true moral agency, while Klara brings into question the nature of love, care, memory, and social recognition as essential qualities of personhood. By drawing upon the frameworks of critical posthumanism and AI ethics, we can find out that the novels are more concerned with whether human beings are capable of retaining a stable and exceptional identity when affect, consciousness, simulation, and ethical agency become entangled rather than on whether machines can be human. As comparison shows that artifice operates as a mirror through which contemporary fiction exhibits the ethical, emotional and ontological fragility of the human self.

Abstract Stretching the integration of renewable energy, energy storage, electric vehicles (EVs) and smart-grid technologies at an unprecedented rate will produce increasingly complex and dynamic power systems that defy conventional optimization and control methods. This paper offers a systematic engineering review of the state of the art and future potential for the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in sustainable and resilient electric power systems, which includes machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning (RL), hybrid AI, explainable artificial intelligence, federated learning (FL), and digital twins (DTs). The review covers their use in renewable energy and load forecasting, energy management, predictive maintenance, demand response, adaptive control, energy storage, smart grid and EV/Vehicle-to-Grid coordination. A single framework based on the grid is presented that integrates predictive intelligence, optimization, adaptive control, cyber-physical systems, explainability, cyber-security, and sustainability in a closed-loop system. The analysis underscores the transformative possibilities of AI in enhancing the use of renewable energy, its efficiency, resilience of the grid and smart decision making. But, deployment needs to address the uncertainties, data quality, computational costs, latency, Cybersecurity, interoperability, scalability, model drift, and regulatory needs. The review also highlights Green AI to tackle the energy and carbon footprint of increasingly large AI models. Lastly, physics-informed and uncertainty-aware AI, safe RL, DT-assisted validation, edge intelligence, FL and real-world benchmarking are identified as key directions for next-generation power systems to remain trustworthy and sustainable.

Background: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy in women globally, accounting for approximately 2.30 million new cases and 666,103 deaths in 2022. Artificial intelligence technologies including machine learning, deep learning, radiomics, and natural language processing have been widely applied across the breast cancer care continuum. However, no systematic review restricted to primary studies with patient-level or image-level data has synthesized evidence spanning all clinical domains simultaneously. Objectives: To evaluate the performance, methodological quality, and clinical relevance of artificial intelligence primary studies across screening and diagnostic imaging, digital pathology, radiomics, perioperative management, prognostic prediction, and natural language processing in breast cancer. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2015 to May 2026. Eligibility was restricted to original primary research reporting patient-level or image-level data; secondary syntheses were explicitly excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Reporting followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Results: Of 5,275 identified records, 17 primary studies met eligibility criteria. In screening mammography (seven studies; n = 7,540 to 144,231 examinations), deep learning achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.876 to 0.939; a randomised trial in 80,033 women demonstrated non-inferiority to double reading with a 44.3% reduction in radiologist workload. In digital pathology (five studies; 270 to 44,732 whole-slide images), deep learning achieved AUC 0.985 to 0.994, exceeding unassisted pathologist performance in lymph node metastasis detection. Magnetic resonance imaging radiomics predicted pathological complete response in HER2-positive breast cancer with AUC 0.80. No breast cancer-specific perioperative primary study met the eligibility criteria. Deep survival networks achieved concordance index 0.626 versus 0.612 for Cox regression in breast cancer cohorts. Natural language processing identified metastatic recurrence in breast cancer clinical records with sensitivity 83% and specificity 73%. Risk of bias was low to moderate for imaging and pathology studies and high for small sample radiomics studies. Density-stratified performance was reported by only two imaging studies, and receptor status prediction from haematoxylin and eosin staining had not been validated as a safe alternative to immunohistochemistry. Conclusions: Artificial intelligence demonstrated clinically meaningful performance across the five domains with eligible primary studies. Breast cancer-specific perioperative and intensive care primary studies were absent, representing the largest evidence gap. External validation, demographic diversity, and prospective clinical integration evidence remained the most consistently identified limitations. Prediction of molecular receptor status without immunohistochemistry requires rigorous prospective safety validation before it can complement standard testing.

documents.abstract: This study examined the influence of Fairness, Transparency, and Accountability [FTA] on student acceptance of Artificial Intelligence [AI] in higher education institutions in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Grounded on an extended Technology Acceptance Model, data were collected from 240 undergraduate students from six universities using a structured 5-point likert scale questionnaire. Descriptive analysis and Pearson correlation were conducted using SPSS v26. Results indicated that students reported moderately high acceptance of AI for learning but low perceptions of fairness, transparency, and accountability. Transparency emerged as the most critical concern, with 45-50% of students reporting limited understanding of AI decision-making processes. Correlation analysis revealed significant positive relationships between all three FTA dimensions and student acceptance. The findings suggest that while perceived usefulness drives initial adoption, ethical concerns may hinder sustainable use. The study recommends that Pakistani HEIs implement bias-free AI systems, provide explainable AI interfaces, and establish clear accountability structures to build student trust. This study contributes to AI ethics literature in the Pakistani context and provides implications for policymakers and university administrators.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping customer engagement, yet its influence on consumer behavior within hospitality and tourism services remains underexplored.This study examines the associations among AI-enabled engagement, digital marketing, and consumer behavior in hospitality and tourism contexts.Survey data were collected from 221 respondents and analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) in an exploratory capacity.The measurement analysis revealed that AI, digital marketing, and consumer behavior are very strongly interrelated: inter-construct correlations were high (AI-DM r = 0.871; DM-CB r = 0.882) and exceeded the square roots of the average variance extracted, so the three constructs did not achieve discriminant validity under the Fornell-Larcker criterion.Rather than interpreting this as a mediation mechanism, the study treats it as a substantive finding: in this hospitality and tourism setting, consumers appear to experience AI, the digital marketing it enables, and their own engagement responses as a single, tightly coupled digitalengagement domain rather than as separable constructs.Model fit was marginal (RMSEA = 0.113; CFI = 0.870), so all relationships are reported as indicative and associational rather than causal.The study contributes contextually by situating AI within hospitality and tourism service ecosystems and by documenting the strong convergence of these digital-engagement constructs, offering guidance for hospitality organizations and advancing discourse on sustainable, human-centered tourism strategies aligned with logistics, informatics, and service science.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Competency-based medical education (CBME) emphasizes clinical reasoning as a core postgraduate competency, yet structured teaching strategies such as SNAPPS remain under-optimized in pediatric postgraduate training. Artificial intelligence (AI) has been proposed as a supervised cognitive scaffold within SNAPPS, but empirical outcome-level evidence, particularly from pediatric postgraduate education in India, is limited. Objective To evaluate the effect of AI-assisted SNAPPS on clinical reasoning, structured case-presentation quality, and knowledge acquisition among pediatric postgraduate residents, and to assess learner and faculty perceptions of the intervention. Methods A prospective, single-arm, within-subject educational interventional study was conducted over six months among 30 pediatric postgraduate residents (10 each from JR1, JR2, and JR3) in the Department of Pediatrics, NKP Salve Institute of Medical Sciences & Research Centre and Lata Mangeshkar Hospital, Nagpur. Following sensitization, all participants underwent baseline assessment, a traditional-SNAPPS teaching phase, and an AI-assisted SNAPPS phase using a standardized SNAPPS-mapped AI prompt protocol with mandatory faculty validation at every step. Outcomes were measured using the Script Concordance Test (SCT), a validated 30-point SNAPPS analytical rubric, a multiple-choice question (MCQ) knowledge test, and five-point Likert perception surveys for residents and faculty. Paired comparisons were analyzed using appropriate parametric and non-parametric tests; p < 0.05 was considered significant. Results Mean SCT scores improved significantly with AI-assisted SNAPPS (12.0 ± 2.0 to 19.6 ± 2.8, p < 0.001), a gain that exceeded the improvement achieved with traditional SNAPPS alone (11.8 ± 2.1 to 15.2 ± 2.5, p < 0.01). The total SNAPPS rubric score rose from 19.1 ± 3.2 to 27.6 ± 2.9 (p < 0.001), with significant gains across all six domains. MCQ knowledge scores improved similarly (12.7 ± 2.5 to 18.8 ± 1.9, p < 0.001). SCT and SNAPPS rubric scores were strongly and positively correlated (r = 0.72, p < 0.001). Both residents and faculty reported significantly higher satisfaction with AI-assisted SNAPPS across every measured domain (all p < 0.001). Conclusion AI-assisted SNAPPS, implemented as a faculty-supervised cognitive scaffold, is feasible, well accepted, and educationally effective for strengthening clinical reasoning, structured presentation and knowledge retention among pediatric postgraduate residents. The model merits validation in larger, multicentric, competency-based curricula.

documents.abstract: This article examines the current state and prospects of using artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in Ukraine's judicial system. It analyses the international and national regulatory and ethical benchmarks for the use of AI in judicial proceedings, in particular the provisions of Opinion No. 26 (2023) of the Consultative Council of European Judges, the European Ethical Charter on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Judicial Systems and their Environment, and the CEPEJ Guidelines on the use of generative artificial intelligence for courts. The article also outlines Ukrainian organisational approaches, notably the Regulation on the Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies by Employees of the Office of the Supreme Court. The main focus is a review of case law on parties' use of generative AI output, references to fictitious court decisions and legal positions, and AI use in drafting judicial acts. The article argues that AI output has no independent evidentiary value and cannot replace the judge’s assessment of evidence, legal analysis or the reasoning of a court decision. It identifies the key risks of using AI: legal ‘hallucinations’, algorithmic bias, opacity, breaches of confidentiality, loss of professional autonomy, and unequal access to technology. Effective integration of artificial intelligence technologies into Ukraine’s judicial system requires not only the formal enshrinement of relevant rules, but also the development of a coherent institutional culture of responsible use. The introduction of AI must be accompanied by uniform methodological guidelines for courts and participants in the judicial process, improved systems for verifying the authenticity of electronic sources, and mechanisms for verifying results obtained using generative models. Ensuring the digital literacy of judges, court staff, lawyers and other participants in the administration of justice is of particular importance, as it is precisely their level of awareness that determines the limits of the safe and ethical use of such technologies. At the same time, it is emphasised that the digitalisation of the justice system must not lead to the devaluation of the human element, a decline in trust in the judiciary, or the erosion of guarantees of a fair trial. The article concludes that the acceptable model for Ukraine is the assistive use of AI, under which technology supports administrative, analytical and information processes but does not take over the functions of the judge. It proposes ways of improving the legal framework: statutory definition of permitted and prohibited uses of AI, the introduction of standards for disclosing its use, and the provision of algorithmic audits, professional training for users and safeguards ensuring effective human oversight.

documents.abstract: Abstract Nigeria has the world’s largest electricity-access deficit, and unreliable grid supply drives demand for solar systems and for dependable after-sales technical support. This report examines how artificial intelligence can strengthen the technical support function of GVE Projects Ltd, a Nigerian solar energy company whose public contact model relies on telephone, e-mail and short online forms. It analyses the current support process and compares it with three reference cases: M-KOPA, Huawei FusionSolar smart diagnostics and GVE’s own pay-as-you-go mini-grids. Technical support is treated as a decision system, in which each contact ends in self-resolution, remote fix, field dispatch or specialist escalation. AI is introduced only where it improves one of these decisions and a human can override it. The report proposes a phased, human-supervised system with five architectural layers: WhatsApp-first customer intake, retrieval-augmented knowledge answers, rule-and-model fault triage with a confidence-gated decision rule, and optional telemetry-based predictive maintenance. The design includes an ArchiMate enterprise-architecture model, key performance indicators, a work breakdown structure, a twelve-month plan, a feasibility study, an ISO 31000:2018 risk evaluation and a five-year economic assessment. Because GVE’s internal data were unavailable, the as-is process and the economic model rest on public sources and stated assumptions, and a sensitivity analysis tests them. The report concludes that a narrow, compliance-first deployment under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 is feasible, and that its success depends more on data quality and staff adoption than on the choice of AI model.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is being integrated into medical education globally, yet evidence from sub-Saharan Africa remains sparse. Postgraduate medical training institutions in this region face distinctive cultural, resource and infrastructure constraints that may shape how educators and trainees engage with AI. This study examined knowledge and self-reported use of AI among postgraduate medical residents and faculty in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted across three postgraduate medical training universities in Dar es Salaam the Aga Khan University (AKU), Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences (MUHAS), and Hubert Kairuki Memorial University (HKMU). A census sampling approach was used, targeting all available residents and faculty. Data was collected via an online structured questionnaire assessing AI knowledge, exposure, and self-rated competence. Knowledge scores were derived from a ten-item questionnaire and compared across groups using Welch's t-test and multivariable linear regression to determine association with knowledge scores. Results A total of 155 participants participated in the study (116 residents, 39 faculty). Mean age group was 31–40 years. Formal AI training was rare (7.1%), yet 80.0% reported using AI in teaching or learning activities. Residents used AI substantially more than faculty (65.8% vs. 14.2%). Overall objective knowledge was moderate (mean score 59.0%, SD 18.2%), with no significant difference between residents and faculty (p = 0.623). Specialty was also associated with knowledge scores, with medical and radiology specialties outperforming non-clinical specialties Self-rated knowledge at Level 5 was the only independent predictor of higher objective scores in multivariable analysis (β = 0.151; 95% CI 0.022–0.302; p = 0.049). Conclusions AI use is widespread among postgraduate trainees in Dar es Salaam despite minimal formal training. Knowledge gaps are evident, particularly around foundational AI concepts. Self-perceived competence, rather than professional role or formal training, predicted objective knowledge. These findings underscore the need for structured, contextually adapted AI literacy curricula within postgraduate medical education in Tanzania and similar settings.

documents.abstract: Rising imaging workload and a shortage of radiology specialists have driven interest in artificial intelligence (AI) to improve diagnostic speed and accuracy. This systematic review, without meta-analysis, describes how AI affects diagnostic accuracy and operational efficiency compared with human interpretation in diagnostic radiology. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) and Cochrane guidance, PubMed, ClinicalKey, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar were searched on 11 April 2026 for studies published from January 2019 onwards. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and a Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2)-based risk-of-bias assessment. Twenty-one studies were included: 11 compared standalone AI with human readers, six compared AI-assisted with unassisted readers, and four reported both; 18 evaluated task-specific image-analysis AI and three evaluated generative AI models. Because no subgroup was homogeneous enough to pool, we synthesised results narratively and stratified them by comparison type, AI category, imaging modality, and study quality. Standalone image-analysis AI achieved high sensitivity for fractures and selected chest findings but performed less well on subtle findings and lower-quality images, and in one computed tomography-referenced comparison a radiologist outperformed AI. AI assistance improved reader performance more consistently, particularly among less experienced readers. Generative models did not reach specialist performance on complex tasks. Efficiency gains were concentrated in normal studies, and the only randomised trial found lower mammography screen-reading workload with similar early screening performance. No study assessed patient outcomes, and 18 of 21 studies were retrospective. This evidence supports AI only as a supervised, complementary tool; improvements in diagnostic accuracy should not be equated with clinical benefit.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become an important tool in social media marketing, enabling businesses to deliver personalized content and enhance consumer engagement. At the same time, growing environmental awareness has increased interest in green products. This study develops a conceptual framework to explain the relationship between AI-driven social media marketing, consumer trust, and green purchase intention in Uzbekistan. Based on recent literature, the proposed framework suggests that AI-driven social media marketing strengthens consumer trust and positively influences consumers' intention to purchase green products. The study contributes to the green marketing literature by integrating these constructs into a unified conceptual model and provides a theoretical foundation for future empirical research in Uzbekistan. Abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence, especially Generative AI, is really changing how we work and what employment looks like. While these AI technologies can boost productivity and enhance decision-making, they might also lessen the need for human workers in some roles, leading to layoffs and job losses. This shift has sparked worries about job security, potential layoffs, the need for reskilling, and whether current labor laws are adequate. This research examines whether the safeguards provide under Chapter V-B of the Industrial Disputes Act from 1947 are enough to protect employees whose jobs are impacted by automation and tech advancements. It zooms in on key legal protections related to layoffs, notice periods, compensation, required government approvals, and other employee safeguards. Additionally, it looks at the challenges posed by Generative AI, especially how tech changes can shift job roles, cut down the demand for certain skills, or even render some positions obsolete. The study takes a doctrinal and qualitative approach, pulling from a variety of sources like legislation, court rulings, academic research, government documents, and insights into AI, automation, and employment. It also examines the Industrial Relations Code of 2020 to grasp how India's labor law framework is evolving in light of technology. The findings indicate that while current labor laws do offer crucial protections during layoffs, they might not fully tackle the issues brought on by AI-related job changes. There's a strong suggestion that more focus is needed on reskilling, redeploying, transparency, and providing support during transitions before any layoffs occur. Therefore, the study advocates for a more employee-centered approach, encouraging employers to prioritize reskilling and redeployment ahead of layoffs, while also balancing tech advancements, business demands, and employee rights. Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) extends conventional predictive and generative AI by enabling systems to pursue goals through reasoning, planning, information retrieval, memory, tool use, and interaction with clinical workflows. These capabilities create new opportunities for medicine but also a distinct evaluation problem: the reliability of an agent cannot be inferred from the accuracy of its underlying model or final answer alone. Errors may arise during information retrieval, tool use, state updates, inter-agent communication, or autonomous action and may propagate across a clinical workflow. This critical review examines approaches for evaluating and clinically validating agentic AI in medicine. Existing frameworks, including TRIPOD+AI, CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT-AI, DECIDE-AI, STARD-AI, FUTURE-AI, and Good Machine Learning Practice, provide important foundations but were not primarily designed for systems with persistent state, repeated actions, tool use, and multi-agent interaction. Emerging agent benchmarks increasingly address interactive tasks, tool use, trajectory reliability, and adversarial testing. We propose a five-level evaluation framework spanning model, agent, trajectory, system, and clinical outcome, together with a clinical validation ladder progressing from component testing and simulation to retrospective evaluation, prospective silent deployment, supervised clinical use, bounded action, and post-deployment surveillance. Key gaps include standardized trajectory metrics, evaluation of correlated multi-agent errors, autonomy-aware validation, human–agent performance, and lifecycle monitoring. Radiotherapy is used as a high-stakes clinical exemplar. We argue that agentic AI should be evaluated as a dynamic sociotechnical system and that clinical evidence must extend beyond accuracy toward behavioral reliability, safety, and demonstrated clinical benefit.

documents.abstract: This study examines the determinants of ethical artificial intelligence (AI) adoption among university students by integrating the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and Digital Divide Theory. Specifically, this study investigates the effects of digital literacy, social influence, and digital divide on ethical AI adoption, as well as the moderating role of digital divide in the relationships between digital literacy, social influence, and ethical AI adoption. A quantitative survey was conducted involving 408 university students in Indonesia. The data were analyzed using regression analysis, supported by reliability and validity tests, correlation analysis, Gaussian copula endogeneity check, Harman’s single-factor test, non-response bias test, and simple slope analysis. The findings show that digital literacy has a positive and significant effect on ethical AI adoption, indicating that students with stronger digital literacy are more likely to use AI critically, responsibly, and in accordance with academic integrity. Social influence also has a positive and significant effect, suggesting that lecturers, peers, academic norms, and institutional guidance play an important role in encouraging responsible AI use. Digital divide-related conditions are also significantly associated with ethical AI adoption, highlighting the importance of access, capability, and digital support in AI-supported learning. However, the moderating effects of digital divide are not statistically supported. These findings suggest that digital divide functions more as a direct contextual factor than as a moderating variable. This study contributes to the literature on AI adoption in higher education by emphasizing that ethical AI adoption is shaped by individual digital competence, social-academic support, and inclusive digital conditions. The findings also imply that universities need to strengthen digital literacy, develop clear AI-use guidelines, and reduce digital access gaps to promote ethical and inclusive AI adoption.

Search and discovery on the 2026 internet is broken for three groups: users who want to find real businesses and resources, small businesses who want to be found, and honest affiliate operators who want to earn from genuine recommendations. Search engines rank results by signals that reward scale, not quality. A local hardware store cannot outrank a content farm that produces ten thousand SEO-optimized pages per day with large language models. Paying for search advertising puts small businesses into bidding wars against companies with orders-of-magnitude larger budgets. Social media demands constant content production — videos, posts, engagement farming — work that has nothing to do with the actual service the business provides. Review platforms are corrupted. Fake reviews, review bombing, pay-to-play visibility schemes, and extortion dynamics have made star ratings unreliable. Users append "reddit" to their search queries as a trust signal, but Reddit itself is degrading as it monetizes and as marketers infiltrate communities. AI answer engines attempt to solve the problem by synthesizing responses, but they draw from the same polluted index and introduce hallucination risk. The underlying data is compromised. No amount of summarization fixes a contaminated source. Honest affiliate operators face the same structural disadvantage. An operator who genuinely tests products and recommends what they believe in cannot compete on volume against content farms that rewrite product descriptions and stuff affiliate links without touching the products. The algorithm cannot distinguish the two. The content farm wins on output volume every time. Three intermediaries sit between a person and a useful resource: algorithmic ranking that rewards manipulation, centralized moderation that makes uniform visibility decisions for all users, and review systems that are themselves a manipulation surface. All three are failing.

Abstract Can an artificial intelligence (AI) system perform the emotional labor of teaching, or can it only reproduce emotional labor's outward signs? In this article, I argue that the latter does not by itself justify the former. Emotional labor in education includes surface acting, but it still presupposes an agent capable of emotion, self‐regulation, and responsibility within a pedagogical relation. Its educational value can also depend on students' reasonable perception that care is not wholly fabricated. I develop this claim through selected debates about machinic emotion from 1950 to 1996. Ziff, Smart, and Putnam dispute whether feeling requires biological life or can be attributed through organized behavior; Weiss, Scriven, and Danto test whether relation, honesty, and language can evidence machine emotion; and Dyer, Ortony et al., and Arbib contest whether computational appraisal can capture embodied affect. These debates do not supply a historical test that contemporary systems must pass. They expose three still‐relevant justificatory questions about ontology, evidence, and embodiment that divide educational critics and technologists. This article uses those questions to distinguish computational representations and simulations of emotion from warranted claims that a system has emotion and performs emotional labor. The result is a shared vocabulary for evaluating affective AI in education and for identifying which forms of pedagogical care cannot simply be inferred from emotionally convincing output.

documents.abstract: The world economy is in the era of the fourth industrial revolution and digital transformation, which has and will continue to affect all spheres of human life. The invention of artificial intelligence (AI) is the result of the above-mentioned process, and it is important to know how to use it correctly. On the one hand, if employers require employees to use various artificial intelligence programs, there is heated discussion in educational institutions about students' improper use of these tools, which leads to a decrease in critical and analytical thinking among young people. It is worth noting that world-renowned universities are seeking to adopt internal regulations on the use of artificial intelligence independently; however, it is important to strike a balance that ensures the training of highly qualified, analytical, and critical-thinking students while equipping them with the technological skills necessary for employment. Research on this topic at various universities worldwide shows that the use of artificial intelligence is effective in some courses, such as English-as-a-foreign-language instruction. However, in preparing a master's or doctoral thesis, which must be original research based on conclusions formulated by the student, the intensive use of AI will not have the desired effect. It is noteworthy that Ivane Javakhishvili Tbilisi State University has developed an AI Strategy 2026-2029, within the framework of which the results of the survey of teachers and employers conducted coincide with the conclusions of similar studies conducted abroad. documents.abstract: Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3×, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20–30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.

This record contains the English translation of sustentabilidade cognitiva — Interação Humano-Máquina, version 1.0, originally published in Portuguese on 31 October 2026: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23846541. The translation was prepared with artificial intelligence assistance on 1 November 2026. This is a theoretical-conceptual preprint and has not undergone peer review. This article presents the conceptual architecture of cognitive sustainability in Human–Machine Interaction developed within the QU and QUEaSTION programme. The guiding question is how intelligibility, autonomy and the conditions for recognition can be preserved when people and systems participate in addressing a dilemma. The approach connects an author-created map of the cognitive process with the current programme manuscripts and selected literature on automation and interaction. The account relates dilemmas, areas of life, roles, actors, SER–TER–ESTAR (being, having and situated states), field influences, preservation, prioritisation, recognisable capacities, applied skills, memories, permission, action and outcomes. It defines QU as the semantic organisation of capacities recognised when weighing dilemmas in complex systems and explains the role of the SEM framework in preserving the meanings being compared. It presents state transformations, the PAC, PAI and PIR patterns, and the distinction between Projected Outcome, Expected Outcome and Produced Outcome. QUEaSTION supports the traceable reconstruction of these relationships; QUIA constitutes a line of technical development. A fictional example of digital scheduling illustrates the scope of the proposal. The contribution consists in organising the framework and delimiting questions for further conceptual development and subsequent empirical investigations.

Corporate social responsibility (CSR) has historically been treated as a discretionary activity outside the realm of strategic management. However, over time CSR has gained traction as a necessary addition to any organisation with positive impact on the firm’s bottom line. Despite this progress, how CSR affects financial performance is not well understood, especially in an emerging- market manufacturing setting. This study investigates CSR’s impact on financial performance for Malaysian manufacturing firms while testing employee engagement as a mediating variable and job autonomy as a moderating condition. Five hypotheses were formulated on the basis of Stakeholder Theory, Social Exchange Theory, and Self-Determination Theory; direct effects of CSR on employee engagement and financial performance, the indirect effect of employee engagement on financial performance, mediation of employee engagement, and moderation of job autonomy were investigated. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional design was utilised. Participants were Malaysian employees working in manufacturing firms who completed a questionnaire. 384 completed questionnaires were collected from a sample of 500 resulting in a response rate of 76.8%. Data were analysed through descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, multiple regression, and conditional process analysis with PROCESS Model 7 using 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results found CSR to have a positive and significant effect on financial performance and employee engagement. Employee engagement had a positive and significant effect on financial performance and fully mediated the relationship between CSR and financial performance. Job autonomy was found to have no significant effect on the relationship between CSR and employee engagement but was found to have a positive and significant relationship with employee engagement. This study contributes to the field of CSR by providing evidence that employee engagement serves as an important internal mechanism through which responsible organisational practices affect financial performance. The findings of this study show that job design may play an important role in manufacturing contexts where there are more formal procedures and requirements for operation.

This study aimed to investigate the effect of students’ conceptions of feedback on their cognitive engagement. Although student cognitive engagement is an extensively researched construct, it is still developing, and various areas remain to be explored one of which is the assessment context for student engagement. Educational researchers have highlighted that investigating the relationship between assessment and student engagement is crucial. To collect data for the constructs, a survey methodology was employed using a convenience sample of 499 university students from six public and private institutions. Two validated instruments the Students’ Conceptions of Feedback (SCoF) inventory and Cognitive Engagement sub-scales from Attitudes Towards Mathematics (ATM) were administered after obtaining formal permission from the developers. Hypotheses were derived from an extensive literature review. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) via SmartPLS 3 was utilized for statistical analysis. The findings revealed a statistically significant positive effect of SCoF on cognitive engagement.

Purpose: This study aimed to design an artificial intelligence–based cognitive empowerment package for enhancing entrepreneurial skills in gifted and creative adolescents through the qualitative identification and integration of relevant cognitive, psychological, motivational, interpersonal, and technological components. Methods and Materials: The study employed a qualitative exploratory-developmental design. Data were obtained through an analytical review of relevant literature, examination of previous student entrepreneurship workshop experiences, and semi-structured interviews with students, mentors, workshop facilitators, and accelerator managers selected through purposive sampling. Data collection continued until conceptual saturation was achieved. Interview transcripts, field observations, documentary evidence, and analytical notes were examined using thematic analysis. Findings: The qualitative analysis indicated that sustained entrepreneurial action among gifted and creative adolescents depends on a multidimensional configuration of entrepreneurial intention and identity, self-efficacy, opportunity recognition and problem identification, executive functioning, tolerance of ambiguity, applied creativity, fear of failure and perfectionism, intrinsic motivation and psychological ownership, teamwork and psychological safety, proactive agency, resilience, future orientation, and reflective readiness to use artificial intelligence. The findings further suggested that entrepreneurial difficulties differ across adolescents and therefore require profile-based rather than uniform intervention. Integration of the themes resulted in a six-session package encompassing profile awareness and goal setting, problem identification and value creation, conversion of ideas into action plans, presentation and feedback utilization, teamwork and agency, and final presentation with a continuation plan. Conclusion: The findings suggest that entrepreneurial empowerment in gifted and creative adolescents should extend beyond creativity and business knowledge by strengthening the cognitive and psychological capacities required to transform ideas into sustained action, while using artificial intelligence as a supervised reflective and personalized learning support rather than as a substitute for adolescent judgment and agency.

The primary objective of the present study was to design and explain an entrepreneurship model for artificial intelligence–based businesses, with a focus on the information and communications technology and computer software industries in knowledge-based companies located in Tehran Province. In terms of purpose, the study was applied, and in terms of approach, it was a qualitative study employing a sequential exploratory design. In the qualitative phase, grounded theory was applied using the systematic approach to identify and conceptualize the dimensions, components, and relationships among the variables affecting AI-based entrepreneurship. The qualitative research field consisted of senior and middle managers, specialists, experts, and experienced employees working in the information and communications technology and computer software industries of knowledge-based companies in Tehran Province. Participants were selected through purposive sampling, which continued until theoretical saturation was reached. Qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using MAXQDA 2024. To enhance the credibility and trustworthiness of the data, triangulation and Lincoln and Guba’s criteria, including credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability, were employed. The findings indicated that the entrepreneurship model for AI-based businesses consists of an interconnected set of causal conditions, contextual conditions, intervening conditions, strategies, and consequences. The causal conditions included factors such as market needs and technological gaps, entrepreneurial opportunity recognition, and customers’ digital preferences, all of which played a fundamental role in the formation of AI-based entrepreneurship. The contextual conditions included the need to establish a knowledge-based ecosystem, policymaking and regulations, financial capabilities and initial investment, advanced technological capacities, specialized human capital, team competencies, and intraorganizational collaboration. Intervening conditions, including legal and regulatory constraints associated with sensitive data and cybersecurity, as well as economic restrictions and sanctions, were also found to affect the development of entrepreneurship. According to the findings, the key strategies were the development of strategic collaborations, product development and upgrading, digital marketing and market penetration, and human capital empowerment. Finally, the consequences of implementing the model included economic and financial maturity, the development of technological authority, social and employment effects, digital transformation in upstream industries, and software export development.

documents.abstract: The rapid development of digital technologies is transforming modern economies by creating new mechanisms of production, distribution, consumption, and public administration. This article examines the theoretical foundations and current trends of the digital economy, focusing on the experience of the Republic of Uzbekistan. Particular attention is given to the "Digital Uzbekistan – 2030" strategy, digital infrastructure, e-government, digital finance, e-commerce, the IT sector, and human capital development. The study applies systematic, comparative, and institutional approaches, as well as the analysis of statistical and regulatory information. The findings show that Uzbekistan has established important institutional and technological foundations for digital transformation. However, challenges remain, including the digital divide, a shortage of qualified specialists, cybersecurity risks, unequal regional access to digital infrastructure, and regulatory gaps. The study proposes strengthening digital infrastructure, developing digital skills, expanding the application of artificial intelligence and big data, supporting digital entrepreneurship, and promoting international digital integration. Informal digital learning of English (IDLE) — learners' self-organized engagement with English through short videos, social media, streaming, gaming, and generative AI outside the classroom — has accumulated a large body of empirical research over the past decade, yet its affective and individual-difference correlates have never been quantitatively synthesized. Existing meta-analyses address only overall effects on achievement, and narrative reviews of emotion and individual-difference variables have pooled no effect sizes. This preregistration reports a three-level meta-analysis that (1) estimates the strength of association between IDLE and positive emotions, negative emotions, and individual-difference variables; (2) tests whether the association with positive emotions is stronger than that with negative emotions, as predicted by broaden-and-build and control-value theories; and (3) explores whether the affective pathway is conditional on trait-like individual differences. Ten sources (Web of Science, ERIC, PsycINFO, OpenAlex, ScienceDirect, Taylor & Francis, Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, CNKI, Scopus) will be searched for correlational studies published from 2014 onward. Effect sizes (Pearson's r, Fisher's z-transformed) will be modeled with three-level random-effects models cross-validated by cluster-robust variance estimation, with seven prespecified moderators and publication-bias correction (PET-PEESE). Expected outcomes are the first preregistered, effect-size-level synthesis of the IDLE–affect/individual-difference literature, clarifying whether IDLE works through feelings or through traits.

Dynamic PGA: Progressive Boundary Formation extends the Dynamic Personalized Guidance Architecture (Dynamic PGA) framework by examining how personalization, trust, human agency, and boundaries should develop together in adaptive AI experiences. As AI systems become increasingly personalized, usefulness depends not only on what an AI system learns about an individual, but also on understanding what information should not be disclosed, reused, inferred, or carried into another context. This paper introduces Progressive Boundary Formation as a human-centered process through which individuals can recognize, communicate, test, and revise personal, relational, professional, and organizational boundaries as their interaction with AI develops. The framework considers the transition from private AI-assisted exploration to consequential human action, including communication, publication, professional activity, and interactions involving other people. It proposes that boundary awareness should develop alongside personalization and trust rather than appearing only as a static privacy setting or late-stage safeguard. Progressive Boundary Formation is presented as a conceptual extension of Dynamic PGA and its broader goal of creating AI experiences that adapt with the human while preserving human judgment, agency, relationships, and appropriate boundaries. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into English language learning through tools that provide adaptive learning, automated feedback, and personalized support. Although previous studies have examined the educational benefits of AI-powered tools, relatively little is known about how English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students experience these technologies and how their perspectives can inform the design of learner-centered Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS). This study explored EFL students’ experiences, perceived benefits, challenges, and expectations regarding AI-powered tools for English language learning. A qualitative research design was adopted using semi-structured interviews with nine Vietnamese university EFL students, and the data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings showed that participants experienced AI-powered language learning tools as adaptive, feedback-oriented, and engaging. They particularly valued immediate feedback, flexible learning opportunities, and gamified features, which they associated with greater confidence, motivation, and learner autonomy. At the same time, participants expressed concerns about over-reliance on AI, the contextual and cultural appropriateness of AI-generated feedback, and data privacy and security. Participants also envisioned future ITS as more conversational, personalized, and culturally responsive systems that could better address individual learning needs. Overall, the findings suggest that participants viewed AI as a valuable learning support while emphasizing the importance of independent learning, teacher guidance, and contextual relevance. The study offers preliminary design implications for learner-centered ITS by highlighting the importance of incorporating learners’ experiences and expectations into future AI-supported language learning systems.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Clinical reasoning for unstructured problems—those lacking clearly defined initial conditions, standard protocols, or singular correct solutions—remains a persistent challenge in medical education. While artificial intelligence (AI) tools have shown promise in structured knowledge tasks, their integration into frameworks designed for unstructured clinical reasoning remains underexplored. Methods A systems thinking assessment framework was adapted for medical education and validated through expert review and inter-rater reliability testing (ICC = 0.801, 95% CI: 0.725–0.866). Fifty-five medical students were randomly assigned to three groups: an AI-assisted learning group (AIL, n = 18) using ChatGPT 4.0 as a guided reasoning aid, a conventional learning group (CL, n = 18) using textbooks and non-AI online resources, and a manual group (MG, n = 19) without any supplementary tools. All participants responded to the same unstructured clinical case comprising seven tasks (Q1–Q7), each scored on a 0–3 scale by five blinded raters. As an exploratory benchmark, ChatGPT 4.0 responses to the identical case were independently scored using the same framework to characterize the AI model's performance profile and limitations. Results The AIL group achieved the highest mean total score (12.11 ± 1.78), significantly outperforming the CL group (8.94 ± 1.08, p < 0.0001) and the MG (9.97 ± 2.37, p < 0.01). Significant advantages were observed in Q2 (information needs), Q5 (scenario development), Q6 (challenges), and Q7 (unintended consequences). Subgroup analysis revealed no significant interaction between learning tools and baseline academic performance (F = 0.213, p = 0.930, η² = 0.018), suggesting consistent benefits across GPA levels. The ChatGPT 4.0 benchmark produced uniformly identical scores (total score 16.5 across all trials), revealing characteristic limitations in response variability and template dependency. Conclusions An AI-assisted learning framework grounded in a validated systems thinking assessment tool can enhance medical students' clinical reasoning for unstructured problems, with effects that appear independent of baseline academic performance. The ChatGPT benchmark highlights both the capabilities and the rigidities of current AI models, underscoring the need for hybrid human–AI collaboration rather than AI substitution in clinical reasoning education. documents.abstract: In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in research involving human participants has gained popularity in clinical and biomedical research domains, more so in advance economies than in low medium income countries (LMIC) like Cameroon. AI is transformative in its ability to perform faster repetitive tasks, analyze large amounts of data, and potentially leading to enhance clinical research decision-making. As with all research involving human participants, research using AI should be in compliance with ethical principles and subject to regulatory guidelines for better protection of volunteering research participants. The use of AI in research involving human participants presents new ethical and regulatory challenges, including those related to privacy and data confidentiality, transparency, amplification of bias, and implications for maintaining human autonomy and oversight. Existing guidelines of most research ethics committees relating to digital health technology evaluation for human research are not up-to- date to address AI evaluation in clinical research. In view of providing a regulatory compliant structure that protects the human participant’s privacy and mitigation of bias Sub-Saharan African countries have an obligation to update their standard operating procedures to integrate aspects for evaluating AI research. There are however, a few existing guidelines from developed countries like the US and Canada that provide the ethical foundations for the use of AI in clinical research. Tools are still required to enhance the protocol review process by the research ethics committees charged with ensuring consistency, efficiency and sustainability across institutions, to reflect accepted standards of ethical research review oversight. This document aims to focus on AI contributions in clinical research, challenges and adopted guidelines for evaluation of AI-driven clinical research. This is in view of providing support for Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) and other ethics advocacy institutions with the awareness and practical friendly user steps to identify, assess, and mitigate potential risks to participants in an AI-driven research, during the ethical review process.

documents.abstract: Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency up to 5.0x. The improvements also transfer to 4 other LLMs and to 6 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. Analysis shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better exploration and exploitation for evolutionary discovery.

Abstract Introduction Librarians' readiness for metaverse technology in Nigerian universities of technology is not well documented. This study aimed to assess librarians' awareness, digital skills, perceived infrastructure, organizational support, and challenges regarding metaverse technology in Federal Universities of Technology in Nigeria, and to examine the relationships between awareness and digital skills and between infrastructure and organizational support. Methods This cross-sectional survey was conducted between April and July 2026 in six Federal Universities of Technology in Nigeria. Academic librarians in these universities who agreed to participate were included, and incomplete questionnaires were excluded. Data were collected with a validated online questionnaire using four-point scales. Descriptive statistics were used with a criterion mean of 2.50, and Pearson correlation was used to test the hypotheses at a 0.05 significance level. Results A total of 103 librarians were included. Overall, 97 (94.2%) reported very high or high awareness of the metaverse concept. While 91 (88.3%) reported being able to operate metaverse access devices, 29 (28.2%) reported being able to upload library content. Reliable internet connectivity was reported by 87 (84.5%), and augmented reality devices by 27 (26.2%). Inadequate training was the most highly rated challenge, reported by 98 (95.1%). Awareness was correlated with digital skills (r = 0.49, p < 0.001), and infrastructure with organizational support (r = 0.38, p < 0.001). Conclusion Librarians appeared to be aware of metaverse technology, but their skills and resources seemed better suited to accessing virtual environments than to delivering library services within them. Introduction The metaverse refers to a persistent, shared multiuser virtual environment that merges physical reality with digital virtuality, in which users interact with one another and with digital content through avatars, supported by virtual, augmented, and mixed reality technologies [1]. The term originated in the 1992 science fiction novel Snow Crash, and the concept has since attracted substantial attention from technology companies and researchers [1,2]. In academic libraries, metaverse technologies have been applied or proposed for virtual tours, exhibitions, information literacy instruction, access to digital collections, and interaction between librarians and users [3,4]. Librarians' awareness of and readiness for metaverse technology have been examined in Thailand, the Gulf region, the United States, and Nigeria [5–8]. Factors reported to influence adoption include librarians' awareness and digital competence; the availability of devices, software, bandwidth, and electricity; and organizational support in the form of funding, training, technical assistance, and policy [9,10]. Privacy, data protection, and cybersecurity have also been identified as implementation concerns [11]. In Nigeria, studies of university libraries have reported variation in digital competencies and technological resources, and interest in metaverse applications alongside limitations in expertise, infrastructure, funding, training, and policy [8,12]. Federal Universities of Technology hold a mandate for technological education and research; however, librarians' awareness, digital skills, and perceptions of infrastructure, organizational support, and challenges relating to metaverse technology in these institutions remain insufficiently documented. This study aimed to assess librarians' awareness, digital skills, perceived infrastructure, organizational support, and challenges regarding metaverse technology in Federal Universities of Technology in Nigeria, and to examine the relationships between awareness and digital skills and between infrastructure and organizational support. Literature Review Awareness of Metaverse Technology among Librarians Proposed library applications of metaverse technology include immersive user engagement and changes to collections and reading spaces [3,13]; virtual, augmented, and mixed reality services [14]; virtual tours, simulations, tutorials, and collaborative spaces [4]; and immersive information literacy instruction [15]. From the user perspective, studies have examined willingness to patronise a metaverse academic library [16], intentions to use metaverse digital library services [17], knowledge exchange through a virtual living library [18], and information needs involving interaction, participation, and user-generated content in metaverse communities [19]. Among librarians, moderate awareness has been reported in Thailand [5] and in Nigeria, where it was accompanied by enthusiasm for adoption [12]. However, the relationship between librarians' awareness and their digital skills has not been examined in Nigerian Federal Universities of Technology. Digital Skills Possessed by Librarians for the Adoption of Metaverse Technology New professional capabilities have been described as necessary for librarians in intelligent library environments [20]. Librarians in the Gulf region have reported substantial familiarity with and interest in metaverse technology, together with barriers related to expertise and technical resources [6]. Positive views of metaverse integration have also been reported alongside gaps in technical expertise [21]. In Nigeria, digital skills have been associated with preparedness for metaverse-enabled services [12], and readiness and digital capacity have been reported to vary across universities [8]. Training has been recommended to address these gaps [4,10,22]. However, existing studies have not distinguished librarians' ability to navigate virtual environments from their ability to create content, retrieve resources, and communicate with users within them. Adequacy of Technological Infrastructure for the Adoption of Metaverse Technology Infrastructure has been identified as a factor in the adoption of metaverse technologies in academic libraries [9] and has been associated with readiness among library professionals in Pakistan [23]. Immersive library applications and scalable metaverse service models require high-capacity connectivity, and internet and infrastructure constraints have been identified as barriers to implementation [4,14]. Reviews of metaverse technologies in libraries have also highlighted implementation constraints [10,22]. In Nigeria, studies have reported uneven technological resources and limited institutional readiness [8,12]. In a related context, facilitating conditions have been associated with librarians' adoption of artificial intelligence [24]. Organizational Support Available for the Adoption of Metaverse Technology Institutional encouragement has been linked with favorable perceptions of metaverse technology among librarians [6], and leadership support has been identified as a component of readiness in Pakistan [23]. In urban libraries in the United States, overall operating expenditure and population served did not explain the application of metaverse-related technologies [7]. In Nigeria, financial and policy constraints have been reported [12]. Recommended measures include professional development [20]; phased implementation, training, and user feedback [4]; and collaboration, policy, and investment [10,22]. Challenges Affecting the Adoption of Metaverse Technology among Librarians. Reported barriers include technical, financial, and ethical concerns in Thailand [5]; connectivity, training, and service delivery [4]; resource and inclusion issues [10,22]; and costs, skills, funding, and readiness in Nigeria [12]. Professional challenges include changes to librarians' roles [20] and changes associated with the convergence of metaverse technology and artificial intelligence [25]. Ethical and security concerns have also been identified [5,22], including cybersecurity and data protection [11]. At the service level, challenges relate to community participation and ownership of information [19] and to the transfer of knowledge exchange into virtual settings [18]. documents.abstract: The integration of AI tools like ChatGPT in language education presents both opportunities and challenges. This mixed-methods study examined the impact of AI on composing strategies and writing performance among 87 upper-intermediate Iranian EFL learners, randomly assigned to a traditional group (n=43) and an AI group (n=44). Both groups completed IELTS Writing Task 2 as pre- and post-tests; the AI group used ChatGPT during the post-test. Concurrent think-aloud protocols, supported by training and video demonstrations, were used to analyze writing strategies, while reflective journals provided qualitative insights. Results showed the AI group achieved significantly higher post-test scores but employed fewer cognitive, rhetorical, metacognitive, communicative, and socio-affective writing strategies, indicating reduced strategic engagement. Thematic analysis revealed learners’ ambivalence: they valued AI for efficiency and personalized feedback but expressed concerns about authenticity, creativity, equity, and academic integrity. The findings suggest that while AI can enhance writing performance, over-reliance may hinder critical skill development. The study advocates for critical AI literacy, emphasizing scaffolded, ethical AI integration aligned with Vygotskian principles. Educators should prioritize personal voice, originality, and higher-order thinking to ensure AI supports, rather than substitutes, the writing process.

documents.abstract: HERMES–AEGIS is a research programme on AI assistance for security teams in industrial plants and other critical infrastructure. It rests on three principles. First, separation by structure: no component that reads AI output is given credentials or a network path to controllers or safety systems, with the plant boundary enforced one way. Second, evidence before conclusions: every claim is tied to its source data and checked before an analyst sees it. Third, intelligence by need: each step uses the least costly sufficient AI model and escalates only when the evidence calls for it. This note sets out the problem, the principles and the current status. HERMES, the reasoning layer, exists as a research prototype exercised with simulated models; AEGIS, a read-only incident-triage application for OT security teams, is in preparation. The note includes one observational result from 7,366 public AI-agent task recordings. It is not a product announcement, makes no claim of validation against real incidents, and makes no claim of compliance with ISA/IEC 62443, NIST guidance or any regulation.

The expanding use of artificial intelligence (AI) in learning has the potential to support students’ learning processes, but its relationship with learning motivation among Pendidikan Guru Sekolah Dasar (PGSD) students still requires investigation. This study aims to analyze the relationship between AI use in learning and learning motivation among PGSD students. The study employed a quantitative approach with a correlational design involving 38 PGSD students. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using Pearson’s product–moment correlation test with SPSS. The results showed a positive and significant relationship between AI use in learning and learning motivation among PGSD students, with a relatively weak correlation (r = 0.352; p = 0.030). Students with higher levels of AI use tended to have higher learning motivation, but this relationship did not indicate causality. This study concludes that AI use in learning is associated with learning motivation among PGSD students. These findings add empirical evidence to research on AI use and learning motivation and can serve as a reference for students and educators in using AI wisely and responsibly as a learning aid. Future research should involve more respondents and examine other factors associated with students’ learning motivation.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in financial services for fraud detection, credit assessment, investment support and digital banking, yet its adoption depends on how users perceive its benefits, risks and trustworthiness. This study examines user perceptions of artificial intelligence in finance, focusing on perceived benefits, perceived risks, trust, explainability, perceived usefulness, adoption intention and perceived effectiveness of financial decisions. A quantitative, cross-sectional design was used, and primary data were collected from 30 respondents through a structured online questionnaire. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach alpha reliability analysis and Spearman rank correlation with Holm adjustment for multiple testing were applied. Perceived benefits and perceived usefulness were positively associated with adoption intention, and adoption intention was positively associated with perceived decision effectiveness; all three associations remained significant after adjustment. The expected negative association between perceived risk and adoption intention was not found, and the trust and explainability hypotheses were not supported. Because the sample was small and concentrated among young respondents in information technology occupations, the findings are exploratory and should not be generalized. The results suggest that perceived value is linked with willingness to use artificial intelligence based financial tools, while the roles of trust and risk need further study.

documents.abstract: The spread of generative artificial intelligence in higher education has begun to change writing classrooms in ways that are not always immediately visible. In second language education, students now revise and refine texts through AI-supported interaction before teachers ever see the final product. This shift raises questions not only about writing quality, but also about how teachers understand, evaluate, and guide the writing process itself. In Japanese writing instruction, where revision often depends on close attention to context, nuance, and interpersonal positioning, these changes carry particular weight. This study examines how ten instructors of Japanese writing at Hanoi University perceive the growing presence of generative AI in their teaching. Based on survey data and qualitative interpretation, the analysis shows that writing instruction remains deeply dependent on teacher labor, especially in areas that require contextual judgment and individualized feedback. At the same time, many instructors described a growing sense of uncertainty. When revision happens through AI outside the classroom, it becomes harder to determine what a student can actually do alone, and this weakens confidence in conventional forms of assessment. Some participants also felt that the teacher’s traditional role as the central source of correction is becoming less stable. Yet this did not lead them to view AI as a replacement. Instead, they emphasized that meaning-making in Japanese writing still relies on human sensitivity to social context and rhetorical intention. Rather than simply introducing efficiency, generative AI appears to be changing the balance of authority in writing education itself.

The incorporation of artificial intelligence into accounting activities has generated new possibilities for process automation, information processing, and professional decision-making support. This study aimed to analyze the perception and use of artificial intelligence tools in accounting decision-making among professionals in Guayaquil. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional study was conducted through a survey administered to professionals working in accounting-related areas. From a population of 307 accountants approached, 222 valid responses were obtained through non-probability convenience sampling. The findings showed that 67.57% of participants considered that artificial intelligence tools improve the accuracy of accounting decisions, while 61.26% reported using them for this type of decision-making. Likewise, 76.58% indicated that these tools reduce the time required to make decisions. A statistically significant association was identified between age and willingness to use artificial intelligence, χ²(3) = 68.63, p < .001, with a Cramer's V of .56. The findings suggest that artificial intelligence has a favorable perception among the professionals studied, although its implementation requires training, human oversight, and ethical criteria.
